extracted.intended_audience: public relations counsels / press agents and PR practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for public relations counsel on creating, packaging, and placing news and ideas across media (newspapers, radio, lectures, motion pictures, advertising, direct mail, etc.), and on professional/ethical obligations to the public and the press.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of news / news value
rubrics_metrics.description: News described (per Mr. Irwin) as "a departure from the established order" and discussed alongside other definitions (e.g., Mr. Given: "Fresh information of something that has lately taken place").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News is characterized by departure from normality but also by timeliness, interest, familiarity of subject/setting/people, effect on personal concerns, and the general importance of persons or activities affected. The page lists four outstanding factors enhancing news value: (1) we prefer to read about things we like; (2) interest increases with familiarity with subject/setting/personae; (3) interest increases with effect on personal concerns; (4) interest increases with general importance of persons/activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truthfulness, accuracy and verifiability
rubrics_metrics.description: Material furnished to the press must be "truthful and accurate" and "verifiable"; editors quickly detect falsehoods and one error can be fatal to PR credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supply only truthful, accurate, and verifiable material; do not deal in spurious goods. The counsel must comply with the highest moral and technical requirements of those with whom he is working to retain editors' trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness
rubrics_metrics.description: Timeliness is a chief element in many definitions of news (e.g., "Fresh information of something that has lately taken place"), although timeliness alone does not make something news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure material has timeliness where appropriate; recognize that timeliness must be combined with other news elements (departure from order, interest) to become publishable news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance and interest to the specific audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Material must have elements of interest required of all news and must "suit the particular needs of each particular newspaper and, even more than that, it must suit the needs of the particular editor in whose department it is hoped that it will be published."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor content to the paper's readership, the department (women's, business, shipping, etc.), and the individual editor's sensibilities; know what each paper and beat values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literary quality / journalistic workmanship
rubrics_metrics.description: The literary quality of the material must be up to the best standards of the profession of journalism; "the writing must be good, in the particular sense in which each newspaper considers a story well written."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare copy as carefully and as accurately verified as if the editor had assigned a special reporter. Good writing and appropriate style for the target medium are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create news (event construction)
rubrics_metrics.description: The public relations counsel must not only supply news—he must create news by staging events or engineering occurrences that have news value (banquets, launches, demonstrations, novelty invitations, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design events with clear, newsworthy manifestations (e.g., bricks as invitations, tactical appeals to higher authorities) to generate press attention; coordinate event form to maximize coverage across mediums.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand requirement for an overt act/manifestation
rubrics_metrics.description: Before a series of events become news they usually have to make themselves noticeable in some more or less overt act; there must be a manifestation or definable shape (bankruptcy filing, fire, arrest, speech, vote, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure that any campaign or story has a concrete, publishable act or document to 'peg' a story; rumors or background knowledge without definitive manifestation rarely become publishable news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Targeting newspaper departments and beats
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspapers have many departments (news, editorial, letters, women's, society, sports, business, financial, shipping, investment, educational, photographic, etc.) and certain places/offices are watched constantly (police, courts, stock exchange, city hall, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match story angle to the appropriate department/beat and exploit the specific sources those beats monitor; use knowledge of beats to anticipate placement and approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience segmentation and direct-by-mail targeting
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct-by-mail and printed word allow classification of individuals by geography, profession, business, religion, economic position, and preferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify your target public into right groups for proper appeals and use lists to reach them directly; treat telegraphic/wireless communications similarly when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of radio / broadcast strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Radio programs vary locally and are controlled by various private or public entities; for partisan matters, controllers insist on presentation of all points of view to avoid charges of propaganda.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Propose symposium treatments for balanced presentation; package information as speeches by reputable persons; use radio as distribution for events (broadcasting speeches) and coordinate with magazines that repurpose broadcasts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lecture platform: strengths and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: The lecture platform's appeal is limited by audience size and physical factors, but it retains importance for staging dramatic events and addressing group leaders who amplify messages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use lectures to reach influential group leaders, to create newsworthy occasions, arrange lecture tours for prominent proponents, and combine lectures with press coverage, advertising, and circularizing to extend reach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising as a paid medium and collaborator
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertising applies to every form of paid space (newspaper ads, billboards, etc.) and has developed its own principles; it is useful for creating markets and propagating ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider advertising among important adjuncts; collaborate with advertising agents to solve particular problems; explore cooperative advertising for joint interests (business groups, governments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the stage and motion picture media
rubrics_metrics.description: The stage offers visual/auditory emphasis and word-of-mouth influence; motion pictures split into feature films (indirect influence) and educational films/newsreels (direct PR use).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work with playwrights/managers to translate ideas into stage action; commission educational films for specific points or arrange newsreel coverage of created events; understand producers' selection processes for feature films.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word-of-mouth and leveraging group leaders
rubrics_metrics.description: Word of mouth is important; group leaders can carry ideas to wider audiences and lend credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and enlist group leaders and influencers to espouse ideas so that personal networks spread the message beyond media placements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate message for medium and editorial department
rubrics_metrics.description: Material must suit the particular needs of each medium and department; what is news for one newspaper may have little interest for another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Customize form, angle, and level of verification to match each medium's expectations and the tastes of the specific editor and department targeted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve editors' trust (long-term credibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Only by presenting news as carefully prepared and accurately verified can the counsel hope to retain "the editor’s faith and trust."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid short-term gains from dubious claims; one discovered falsehood can permanently damage relationships—prioritize accuracy and ethical sourcing to maintain ongoing media relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral and professional obligations as a special pleader
rubrics_metrics.description: As an advocacy profession, public relations must overcome public reluctance and operate with high ethics; new professions must be established by their own energy and sound practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge the partisan nature of PR work but strive to avoid crowd antagonism and accusations of unethical propaganda; act to establish the profession through ethical, competent practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know and exploit diversified approaches across media
rubrics_metrics.description: There are many possible approaches on any subject from both the press standpoint and human psychology; PR counsel should have recourse to diversified methods (press, radio, stage, films, lectures, advertising, direct mail).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correlate media approaches with psychological levers (familiarity, interest, personal effect) and combine mediums to amplify and reinforce the message.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare material to reporter-level standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Material should come to the editorial desk "as carefully prepared and as accurately verified as if the editor himself had assigned a special reporter to secure and write the facts."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include corroborating facts, documents, manifest actions, and clear writing so editors can run copy without extra investigative work; reduce friction for uptake.
